slides.heading: Largest Island
slides.subtitle: AlgoExpert · Hard · Graphs
slides.narration: Let's solve Largest Island, a hard graphs problem. We'll restate the problem, build the intuition, walk through the approach, read the Java solution, and finish with its complexity.

slides.heading: The problem
bullets: Flip at most one water cell to land to maximise the largest 4-connected land island; return its size.
Label islands with ids and sizes first.
slides.narration: Here's the problem. Matrix of 0 (land) and 1 (water). Flip at most one water cell to land to maximise the largest 4-connected land island; return its size. Label islands with ids and sizes first.

slides.heading: Intuition
bullets: Label each island with its size, then for each water cell sum the distinct neighbouring islands plus one.
slides.narration: Label each island with its size, then for each water cell sum the distinct neighbouring islands plus one.

slides.heading: Brute force vs optimal
bullets: Flip each water cell and recount → O((w·h)²)
Label islands once, then check each water cell's distinct neighbours → O(w·h)
Use a set so an island isn't counted twice
slides.narration: Flipping each water cell and flood-filling again is quadratic in the grid size. Label islands once with their sizes, then each water cell just sums its distinct neighbouring islands.

slides.heading: Approach
bullets: 1. Flood-fill to label islands and record sizes
2. For each water cell, collect unique neighbouring labels
slides.narration: Step by step. First, flood-fill to label islands and record sizes. Second, for each water cell, collect unique neighbouring labels. Third, sum sizes plus one. Fourth, take the max.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: 0 = land, 1 = water: flip one 1 to maximise the island
slides.narration: Here zeros are land and ones are water. We may flip one water cell to land; what's the largest island?

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Label islands: A = 3, B = 1
slides.narration: First label each island and record its size: A has three cells, B has one.

slides.heading: Worked example
slides.caption: Flip (1,2): 1 + A + B = 5
slides.narration: Now for each water cell, add one plus the sizes of the distinct islands next to it. Flipping row one, column two joins A and B: five.

slides.heading: Java solution (1/2)
slides.narration: We label each land component with an ID from two upward and record its size. Then for each water cell we collect distinct neighbouring IDs, sum one plus their sizes, and keep the best.

slides.heading: Java solution (2/2)
slides.narration: We label each land component with an ID from two upward and record its size. Then for each water cell we collect distinct neighbouring IDs, sum one plus their sizes, and keep the best.

slides.heading: Complexity
slides.narration: Time is O of w times h. Space is O of w times h.

slides.heading: Edge cases & pitfalls
bullets: Count each neighbouring island once (set of IDs)
slides.narration: Use a set of island IDs so an island touching a cell from two sides isn't counted twice. If there's no water, the answer is the whole grid.
